title: Subgroup Performance
goals: Calculate subgroup results with sample sizes
Distinguish missing evidence from equal performance
Report differences without assigning causes from a table
vocabulary: A defined subset of the evaluated examples
Reporting results separately for defined groups
Which groups and conditions are represented
An observed difference between group results

blocks.title: Subgroup evaluation at a glance
blocks.caption: Changing one B error to a correct result changes its rate from 60 to 40 percent. Small samples can be unstable without making the observed errors unimportant. A missing group has no measured rate, not zero error. Intersections of conditions may be even smaller.

blocks.label: How does correcting one B error affect its rate? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

guided_practice.title: Check sensitivity
guided_practice.prompt: How does correcting one B error affect its rate?
guided_practice.answer: Teacher explanation: B becomes 2/5=40 percent, a 20-percentage-point change from one case.

independent_case.title: Apply independently
independent_case.task: Groups X 1 error/10 and Y 2/4: calculate separate and pooled rates, then state one limit.
independent_case.answer: Teacher explanation: X 10 percent; Y 50 percent; pooled 3/14 about 21.4 percent. Y has only four examples, and the table does not establish a cause.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: Ask for the relevant counts, units, procedure or saved record. For this week: A 2/20=10 percent; B 3/5=60 percent; pooled 5/25=20 percent, a 50-point group gap.
A stronger claim makes a stronger project
Error types, consequences, access, labels and context can differ; a single equality does not establish acceptable treatment.
The new case can be copied from the example
The independent task changes the evidence. Require a fresh explanation: X 10 percent; Y 50 percent; pooled 3/14 about 21.4 percent. Y has only four examples, and the table does not establish a cause.

blocks.text: ML MECHANISM
Input → Model → Evidence
Trace the information, fitted behavior, and evaluation proof separately.
QUESTION  Calculate subgroup accuracy and recall gaps with adequate denominators.
MODEL IDEA  Overall metrics can conceal uneven behavior across meaningful conditions or user groups.
PROOF NEEDED  Use an unseen case, visible calculation, error analysis, and a stated limitation.
UNDER THE HOOD  Daylight: 18/20 correct = 90%; evening: 10/20 = 50%. Accuracy gap = 90% − 50% = 40 percentage points.
Draw a fresh data → model → prediction → evaluation trace:
A closer explanation

Sensor group A has 2 errors in 20 examples and group B has 3 in 5. Error rates are 10 and 60 percent; pooled error is 5/25=20 percent. The group difference is 50 percentage points. B has only five examples, so its rate is sensitive to each individual result.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.
Connect the picture and the explanation
Point to the input, the deciding step and the result in this week’s visual. Explain the same step in ordinary words. A picture helps when you can say what each part represents.
EVALUATION DESIGN
Four Tests, Four Kinds of Evidence
A system is not understood until it survives more than one comfortable example.
NORMAL  Expected data and expected behavior.
BOUNDARY  Value close to a threshold, ambiguous label, or uncertain prediction.
MISSING  Necessary field, label, source, or measurement is unavailable.
SHIFTED  New lighting, species, device, subgroup, or time condition.
RELEASE RULE  Passing one case never proves generalization. Predefine expected behavior for all four categories.
